title: Mathematical Modeling in Infectious Disease Epidemiology: A Systematic Scoping Review of Theoretical Foundations, Structural Typologies, and Applications for Global Public Health (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Mathematical models have become the intellectual infrastructure of modern infectious disease epidemiology. However, the literature on this topic is highly fragmented across different model families, specific pathogens, and methodological niches, lacking a comprehensive and integrative synthesis. OBJECTIVE This systematic scoping review aims to synthesize the theoretical foundations, structural typology, and public health applications of mathematical models in infectious disease epidemiology, while identifying critical methodological gaps to guide future research and practice. METHODS We conducted a systematic scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, updated by Levac et al. and the Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines, reported according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). We searched six electronic databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, MathSciNet, and Google Scholar) for literature published between January 1991 and December 2025. From 4,217 initially identified records, 228 were assessed in full text, and 50 studies were included in the final synthesis. RESULTS The review identified and systematically compared six structural model families: deterministic compartmental, stochastic, network-based, agent-based, statistical/hybrid, and fractional-order. Key epidemiological parameters synthesized included the basic reproduction number (R0), the effective reproduction number R(t), the case fatality ratio (CFR), and the latent and incubation periods. Documented R0 estimates ranged from 1.4-1.6 for pandemic influenza H1N1 (2009) to 12-18 for measles in unvaccinated populations. Applications spanned tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, SARS, MERS-CoV, pandemic influenza, dengue fever, and COVID-19. While 96% of studies transparently described their model structure, only 28% provided code or data for reproducibility. To address a critical gap in behavioral modeling, we propose a parsimonious bio-behavioral dynamic transmission rate (β(t) = max(0, β0 + αt - θI)) that incorporates adherence fatigue and prevalence-elastic risk awareness. The review identified three critical methodological gaps: validation during early outbreak phases, integration of human behavior, and systematic comparisons between model families. CONCLUSIONS Mathematical models are indispensable tools for infectious disease epidemiology, yet their maximum utility depends on robust validation, methodological transparency, and high-quality data. This review provides a comprehensive typological comparison and synthesis of documented parameters while articulating an actionable research agenda prioritizing standardized validation platforms, behavioral integration, and multidisciplinary collaboration for future global health emergencies.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们按照Arksey和O'Malley框架和Joanna Briggs Institute指南进行了系统范围审查,搜索了六个电子数据库,涵盖了1991年1月至2025年12月期间发表的文献。
elements_zh.methods: 审查确定并系统比较了六种结构模型家族:确定性 compartimental、随机、基于网络、基于代理、统计/混合和分数阶。关键流行病学参数包括基本再生数(R0)、有效再生数R(t)、病死率(CFR)和潜伏期和潜伏期。
elements_zh.main_results: R0估计值范围从2009年大流行流感H1N1的1.4-1.6到未接种疫苗人群中的麻疹的12-18。应用范围包括结核病、艾滋病、SARS、MERS-CoV、大流行流感、登革热和COVID-19。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 审查提出了一种简化的生物行为动态传播率(β(t) = max(0,β0 + αt - θI)),该率考虑了依从性疲劳和患病率-弹性风险意识。它确定了三个关键的方法学空白:早期暴发阶段的验证、人类行为的整合以及模型家族之间的系统比较。

elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 只有28%的研究提供了代码或数据以确保可重复性。

full_text: Coroner confirms US measles death while CDC count remains at zero amid row over the fatalities BMJ 2026; 394 doi: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100789 (Published 08 September 2026) Cite this as: BMJ 2026;394:e100789 A child has been confirmed to have died of measles by the coroner of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania—the first such death in Pennsylvania for 35 years.1 It follows intense scrutiny over the case, in which US health officials sought to downplay reports that two recent infant deaths in the county were caused by the disease. Stephen Diamantoni, Lancaster County coroner, told The BMJ that the death of a six week old girl on 18 August was “caused by measles.” The girl also had Amish lethal microcephaly. “The average life expectancy with this condition is 4 to 6 months of age. Because of the compromised state of these children many die of respiratory infections,” Diamantoni said. He first confirmed to US media at the weekend that measles had caused the girl’s death.2 US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who previously referred to “so called measles deaths”3 in Lancaster County, acknowledged and appeared to accept the update on social media.4 As of Tuesday morning, however the US Centers for Disease Control & Prevention (CDC) still had not updated its web page on US measles statistics to include the death.5 A statement on that page simply says that there are currently no death records that indicate measles as the “underlying cause.” It adds that the CDC is developing a new “standardised case definition for deaths due to measles.” The agency does say that there have been 3134 measles cases in the US to date this year, already significantly higher than last year’s total of 2289. The BMJ approached the CDC for comment. The Lancaster County coroner’s update is the latest development in a very public saga around two child deaths in his jurisdiction described as “measles associated” by the Pennsylvania Department of Health in a statement on 25 August.6 On 26 August, Kennedy Jr claimed in a social media post that “the deaths may even have been altogether fabricated” and cited information from the county coroner, which, at the time, did not show any record of measles deaths.7 “I have thoroughly reviewed the case investigation information and sadly can confirm that there were two recent measles associated deaths in Lancaster County,” said Pennsylvania health secretary Debra Bogen in a response on social media posted on 27 August.8 Diamantoni has similarly referred to two child deaths in Lancaster County, the six week old Amish girl and a newborn baby boy who had a ruptured spleen. “Our forensic pathologist . . . felt that this was traumatic and not related to measles, as the spleen was not enlarged or inflamed,” he told The BMJ. “We are continuing our investigation as to what may have caused the laceration.” While Diamantoni suggested the case of the newborn boy was one of the “measles associated” deaths cited by the Pennsylvania Department of Health, he added, “I am uncertain whether the death of the 6 week infant is the [second] death that they referred to.” The BMJ has approached the Pennsylvania Department of Health for clarification. Arguments have erupted on social media over whether the children’s deaths were “measles associated” or “measles caused.” But David Elliman, a community paediatrician and honorary associate professor at University College London, said this is merely “playing with words.” “You wonder how much of this is based on medicine and how much it is based on politics,” he told The BMJ, arguing that the Lancaster County situation was leading to “continued confusion and destruction of trust in what were established bodies.” Elliman pointed out that, because babies are too young to be immunised against measles, the only means of protecting them from this highly contagious disease was through vaccinating older people to establish herd immunity. Vaccination rates for measles are currently falling in the US.9 Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, said unfounded scepticism around the measles vaccine was a cause for concern. “It’s a smouldering situation that is just not getting any better-and that will lead, ultimately, to further deaths,” he said. “Not at a huge rate, but where measles is a significant factor in the outcome.”

full_text: SPECIAL CLINICAL REVIEW PEER-REVIEWED Measles: A resurgent threat and the role of pharmacists in prevention Fawziah Marra BSc(Pharm), PharmD, FCSHP, ACPR, RPh1, Roxane Carr BSc(Pharm), PharmD, FCSHP, ACPR, RPh1,2 Overview Considered eliminated in Canada over 25 years ago, measles has re-emerged as a public health concern due to declining vaccination rates and increased global travel. In fact, recently Canada, and by extension all the Americas, has been stripped of its measles-free certification by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) after failing to curb an outbreak of the virus for 12 consecutive months.1 The majority of the outbreak cases stem from undervaccinated communities in Alberta and Ontario, although cases have been reported in most provinces and territories. To regain its measles elimination status, vac- cination of the population will play a vital role. As accessible health care providers, pharmacists are in a unique position to detect early signs of disease, educate the public, and play a vital role in vaccination programs. Epidemiology The measles virus is a member of the Paramyxoviridae family, which includes mumps, parainfluenza, and respiratory syncy- tial (RSV) viruses.2 Infection with measles results in lifelong immunity.2 Measles is a nationally notifiable disease.3 The live- attenuated vaccine, containing measles only, was introduced into Canadian routine immunization programs in the early 1970s.4 Between 1974 and 1983, a 1-dose combined vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) was introduced. How- ever, Canada moved to the 2-dose MMR vaccine series between 1996 and 1997 with school-based catch-up to ensure chil- 1Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC; 2BC Children’s Hospital, Vancouver, BC Correspondence: Fawziah Marra, (fawziah@mail.ubc.ca). dren had 2 doses.3,4 Between 1970 and 2024, measles cases decreased by more than 99%.4 The success of the 2-dose MMR campaign allowed Canada to achieve measles elimination status in 1998.3 However, spo- radic outbreaks continued to occur, primarily due to the importation of cases from regions of the world with ongoing transmission or transmission from clusters of unvaccinated individuals. From 1998 to 2023, an average of 91 measles cases were reported annually, ranging between 0 and 752 cases (Figure 1).4 Unfortunately, the number of cases in 2025 has increased exponentially.5 As of November 8, 2025, a total of 5208 measles cases were reported by 10 jurisdictions (Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Northwest Territories, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, and Saskatchewan) (Figure 2).6 Most cases occur in children under 5 and adolescents, particularly those unvaccinated or undervaccinated. Transmission Humans are the only reservoir for measles. The basic repro- duction number (R0) is estimated to be between 12 and 18 (i.e., one infected person will go on to infect 12 to 18 other people). This is approximately 10 times higher than for COVID-19 or influenza,7 making measles one of the most infectious known pathogens. The virus primarily spreads through airborne res- piratory droplets and aerosolized droplet nuclei, which can remain infectious in the air or on surfaces for up to 2 hours © Canadian Pharmacists Association (CPhA), 2026. Incubation and clinical presentation Figure 3 shows the clinical progression of measles.2 It typically begins with prodromal symptoms that start 10 to 14 days (range 7 to 23) post-exposure. Prodromal symptoms include fever, as well as cough, coryza (runny nose), or conjunctivitis. A good way to remember the symptoms is fever plus 3C’s. The prodro- mal phase lasts for 2 to 4 days. Diarrhea can also occur during the prodromal stage.8 Two to 3 days after the prodromal symptoms begin, Koplik spots appear, which occur in 50% to 70% of patients (Figure 4). They are highly characteristic of measles and appear as small, white or gray specks on the buccal mucosa, usually opposite the molars.9 They can also appear on the vaginal or gastrointestinal mucosa or the conjunctival folds. Koplik spots typically appear 1 to 2 days before the rash, and their presence can aid in mak- ing a clinical diagnosis earlier.8,9 As the Koplik spots fade, an erythematous maculopapular rash appears, which spreads in a specific order—beginning at the hairline, spreading to the face, C P J / R P C r J A N U A RY / F E B R U A RY 2 0 2 6 r V O L 1 5 9 , N O 1 33 SPECIAL CLINICAL REVIEW FIGURE 3 Clinical course of primary measles infection Permission obtained from Bird C, Dutton F. How to recognise and manage measles. BMJ 2025; 388: e079895. doi:10.1136/bmj-2024- 079895. FIGURE 4 Koplik spots in a patient with measles Reprinted with permission from Aziz J. Rash inside the mouth [Photo]. Am Fam Physician 2017;95(11):729. then the trunk, arms and, lastly, legs. It lasts 4 to 7 days, fading in the same order of appearance.2,4 Health care professionals should consider measles if a child presents with prodromal symptoms, rash, and diarrhea.2,8 Complications and sequelae Complications occur frequently (in up to 30% of cases) and can appear up to 1 month after infection. Complications are more frequent and severe in pregnant people, children un- der 2 years, and individuals who are immunocompromised.4,8 Notably, measles infection in pregnancy is associated with a higher risk of a low-birth-weight infant, premature labour, and spontaneous abortion. Common complications, occurring in approximately 1 in 10 cases, include otitis media, pneumonia, conjunctivitis, and diarrhea.4,10 Less common but severe complications include respiratory failure and encephalitis, which occur at a rate of 1 in 1000.4,8,10 Encephalitis can occur during the first 7 days of infection, 1 to 6 months after infection, or even years after full recovery.9 Death can occur, but it is rare (rate of 1 to 10 in 10,000 cases of measles) and is mainly due to neurologic or respiratory-related complications.11 Measles infection can lead to a number of long-term sequelae,4,10 including blindness, deafness, and permanent neurological sequelae. The latter category includes subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare brain disorder char- acterized by behavioural and intellectual deterioration and seizures, which is often fatal. Diagnosis and laboratory testing The Public Health Agency of Canada states that health care providers should “suspect measles in a patient presenting with a febrile illness and rash, or history suggesting that they are not immune to measles, particularly if they have travelled or are known to have had an epidemiologic link to a measles case or outbreak.”12 Other clinical manifestations, such as the prodrome followed by the rash, the progression of the rash and Koplik spots, should raise clinical suspicion for measles. Currently, there is no point-of-care test for measles. To confirm the diagnosis, 2 clinical specimens, either a nasopha- ryngeal or a throat swab, and urine are required for viral detection by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in addition to serology. This has good sensitivity and specificity for measles detection, particularly within 7 days of rash onset. Measles serology (immunoglobulin M [IgM] and immunoglobulin G [IgG] antibodies) can also be used, but it is not required and may be less reliable in the early stages of the infection. In ad- dition, if the prevalence of measles in the community is low, the positive predictive value of obtaining serology for acute infection (IgM) is decreased significantly. Serological testing may be indicated to determine an individual’s immune status, but testing is not recommended for checking susceptibility be- fore measles vaccination or antibody response after receiving vaccination for measles.13 Infection prevention and control practices Because of the infectiousness of measles, the infection con- trol measures for an active or suspected case include placing a mask on yourself and the patient, isolating the patient with suspected measles into either a private room (if in a commu- nity pharmacy) or a negative-pressure room (in emergency department), and closing the door, ensuring there is a sign on the door. If the pharmacy does not have a private consultation 34 C P J / R P C r J A N U A RY / F E B R U A RY 2 0 2 6 r V O L 1 5 9 , N O 1 SPECIAL CLINICAL REVIEW room, send your patient home wearing a mask. Patients should be instructed to stay at home until their lab results return nega- tive or at least 4 days after rash onset.14 Their exam/clinic room should not be used for 2 hours after the patient has left. If a patient presents with symptoms in the emergency de- partment, notify Infection Prevention and Control, then Public Health, and the Medical Health Officer (MHO). If the patient is in a community pharmacy, call your local health unit and re- port to the MHO. All patient-facing staff must provide evidence of measles immunity, either through 2 MMR vaccinations or a documented positive measles IgG result. Treatment and supportive care Antivirals that target the measles virus are not available. Management is supportive, including adequate hydration and antipyretics to control fever and discomfort. Vitamin A supplementation is recommended for children in resource-limited settings, but it is not routinely used in Canada. Vitamin A deficiency has been linked to delayed recovery and greater complications with measles. Studies conducted in resource-limited countries in the 1980s and 1990s reported that high doses of vitamin A administered orally in 2 daily doses reduced the risk of mortality from measles in children under 2 years of age and shortened the duration of diarrhea and fever by 2 and 1 days, respectively.15 The World Health Organiza- tion (WHO) recommends children diagnosed with measles be given 2 doses of vitamin A supplements. Dosing information can be found in the WHO position paper.16 Given that vitamin A deficiency is uncommon in Canada, routine use of vitamin A in the treatment of measles is not recommended. It may be considered in certain specific situations (such as pre-existing malnutrition) or in severe illness requiring hospitalization. Hospitalization may be required for complications, particu- larly pneumonia or encephalitis. Prevention Vaccination is the key to preventing a measles infection. The recommended age for the first dose is dependent on whether the country has a measles elimination status or not. In coun- tries where measles is endemic, that is, low- to middle-income countries, the first dose is usually given at 9 months of age (can be as early as 6 months).17 In countries with low rates of measles infections, the first dose is given at 12 months of age, as this is the age when maternal antibody levels in the infant will have decreased to a low enough level to optimize the infant’s development of antibodies from the vaccine. The WHO rec- ommends a second dose because 10% to 15% of children who receive only 1 dose do not seroconvert, resulting in a first-dose efficacy of 85% to 90%. With a second dose, efficacy is almost 100%, and lifelong immunity is achieved in most people.8 Dur- ing outbreaks, the WHO recommends an additional dose for children at 6 to 11 months of age. The 2 vaccine products available in Canada are the measles- mumps-rubella (MMR) and combined with varicella (MMRV), which are both live, attenuated vaccines. Note that the MMRV vaccine is authorized for individuals 12 months to less than 13 years of age. The 2 products are considered interchangeable. Routine MMR and MMRV vaccine schedule in Canada18 Children r First dose: 12 to 15 months of age r Second dose: 18 months or 4 to 6 years (depending on province) r Note: If a dose is administered to an infant before 12 months of age due to travel or during an outbreak, it is recom- mended that the infant still receive 2 additional doses, as per the routine immunization schedule. Adults r Two doses of the MMR vaccine are recommended for in- dividuals born on or after January 1, 1970, and for all health care workers born on or after January 1, 1957. Those born earlier are considered immune, as are individuals with a laboratory-confirmed infection or laboratory-confirmed immunity. r Patients with an uncertain immunization history, or those born before 1970 (or before 1957 for health care staff) reporting no history of measles infection, may also be immunized. Measles vaccine before travelling r Early vaccination is strongly recommended for families before travelling to measles-affected areas. r Infants: Children aged 6 to 11 months should be offered an early dose of MMR for protection. This dose will not count towards their series, but it will provide protection against travel-related infections. It will need to be repeated at 12 months of age, as their usual series, which begins at 12 months of age, is started without counting the early dose received. r Young children with 1 dose: Children who are travelling and have received their first dose of measles vaccine at 12 months of age should receive their second dose early, with a minimum interval of 4 weeks after the first dose. r Older children and adults who are travelling and born after January 1, 1970 should be offered an MMR if they are not certain they have had 2 previous doses or have a history of infection. C P J / R P C r J A N U A RY / F E B R U A RY 2 0 2 6 r V O L 1 5 9 , N O 1 35 SPECIAL CLINICAL REVIEW Special considerations It is worthwhile remembering that adults born after 1970 should receive 2 doses if they are unsure of their immunity or if their vaccination records are not available. It is important to note that health care workers, travellers, and post-secondary students require some form of documented immunity, either as documented receipt of vaccines, history of laboratory- confirmed infection, or serological confirmation. The vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromised in- dividuals; susceptible breastfeeding women should receive the MMR vaccine. During a measles outbreak, individuals aged 6 months and older who are susceptible may receive the MMR vaccine. However, if the dose is administered in a child who is 6 months to less than 12 months of age, then 2 additional doses of measles-containing vaccine (given at least 4 weeks apart) must be administered after the child reaches 12 months of age to ensure long-lasting immunity to measles.18 Adverse events and contraindications18 Immunization with a measles-containing vaccine produces mild side effects that occur less frequently than those of a natu- ral infection. They are less frequent with the second dose. Mild reactions include local injection site reactions, such as pain, redness, and swelling, which typically occur 1 to 2 days after vaccination. However, in approximately 5% of children, side effects such as fever, malaise, and a mild rash may develop 1 to 3 weeks after immunization. Parotitis, lymphadenopathy, and joint symptoms can also occur after vaccination. The local reactions of pain, swelling, redness at the injec- tion site, and fever are more common with the MMRV vaccine compared to the MMR vaccine, occurring in 10% of children. In addition to these symptoms, a measles-like, rubella-like, or varicella-like rash can also be seen in 1% to 10% of children afterwards. Serious adverse events and anaphylaxis are infrequent but include immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) that occurs within 6 weeks after immunization, and encephalitis that oc- curs at a rate of 1 per million doses, which is much lower than the rate of natural infection encephalitis, which occurs in 1 per 1000 cases. Febrile seizures following vaccination are observed at a rate of 1 per 2500 doses. This typically occurs when the first MMRV dose is administered to children 12 to 23 months old, whereby the risk of seizure is highest 7 to 10 days post-vaccination. Post-exposure prophylaxis Measles post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) should be consid- ered for individuals at high risk of complications who are not expected to have immunity to measles (i.e., unvaccinated and have never had measles infection). The purpose of PEP is to decrease the likelihood of infection, or if infection does occur, reduce the severity of the disease. Administration of MMR vaccine to non-immune children within 72 hours of exposure to measles has been shown to reduce the risk of developing measles by 83.4% (95% CI 34.4%–95.8%).18 Immunoglobulin administered within 6 days of measles exposure was reported to be 100% effective in preventing measles infection.18 Immunoglobulin is typically administered either intramuscularly or intravenously (depend- ing on the volume of the dose to be administered)…

analysis.summary_en: Studies conducted in resource-limited countries in the 1980s and 1990s reported that high doses of vitamin A administered orally in 2 daily doses reduced the risk of mortality from measles in children under 2 years of age and shortened the duration of diarrhea and fever by 2 and 1 days, respectively.15 The World Health Organiza- tion (WHO) recommends children diagnosed with measles be given 2 doses of vitamin A supplements. Common complications, occurring in approximately 1 in 10 cases, include otitis media, pneumonia, conjunctivitis, and diarrhea.4,10 Less common but severe complications include respiratory failure and encephalitis, which occur at a rate of 1 in 1000.4,8,10 Encephalitis can occur during the first 7 days of infection, 1 to 6 months after infection, or even years after full recovery.9 Death can occur, but it is rare (rate of 1 to 10 in 10,000 cases of measles) and is mainly due to neurologic or respiratory-related complications.11 Measles infection can lead to a number of long-term sequelae,4,10 including blindness, deafness, and permanent neurological sequelae. To confirm the diagnosis, 2 clinical specimens, either a nasopha- ryngeal or a throat swab, and urine are required for viral detection by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in addition to serology. In coun- tries where measles is endemic, that is, low- to middle-income countries, the first dose is usually given at 9 months of age (can be as early as 6 months).17 In countries with low rates of measles infections, the first dose is given at 12 months of age, as this is the age when maternal antibody levels in the infant will have decreased to a low enough level to optimize the infant’s development of antibodies from the vaccine.

title: Timeliness of measles vaccination in selected districts of Oromia Region, Ethiopia – 2021
abstract: Background Delays in vaccination with the first/s dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1, MCV2) increases risk of measles transmission. MCV2 was added to Ethiopia's routine immunization schedule in 2019, administered at age 15 months. We describe age at measles vaccination and characteristics associated with timely vaccination following MCV2 introduction. Methods A secondary analysis from a 2021 cross-sectional household survey of children aged 12–35 months in Oromia, Ethiopia was conducted. MCV vaccination status and age at vaccination were determined from the child's vaccination card. The cumulative card-confirmed vaccination coverage of MCV1 and MCV2 (among children 24–35 months) by age at vaccination was estimated. Among children who received MCV, vaccination timing was classified as early (MCV1: <9 months; MCV2: <15 months), timely (MCV1: 9 to <10 months; MCV2: 15 to <16 months), or delayed (MCV1: ≥10 months; MCV2: ≥16 months). Characteristics associated with timely MCV1 vaccination were analyzed using multivariate logistic regression, with urban/rural stratification. Results Overall, 651 children aged 12–35 months (MCV1) and a subset of 270 children aged 24–35 months (MCV2) were analyzed. Cumulative MCV1 coverage was 59.9% by age 9 months and 76.3% by age 12 months, and MCV2 was 33.0% by age 15 months and 44.8% by age 24 months. MCV coverage was generally higher in urban compared to rural areas. Among vaccinated children, the proportion receiving early, timely, and delayed doses was 30.1%, 44.5%, and 25.3% for MCV1, and 28.6%, 41.2%, and 30.3% for MCV2, respectively. Characteristics associated with timely MCV1 vaccination differed in urban and rural areas, but common themes included increased caregiver immunization awareness and service delivery aspects. Conclusions Although most children who received MCV1 were vaccinated by 12 months, many received delayed doses. MCV2 coverage was low, irrespective of vaccination timing. Findings highlight the importance of routine catch-up vaccination policies and guidance, and the need for tailored strategies in urban and rural settings to improve MCV coverage and timely vaccination.

abstract_original: Background Delays in vaccination with the first/s dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1, MCV2) increases risk of measles transmission. MCV2 was added to Ethiopia's routine immunization schedule in 2019, administered at age 15 months. We describe age at measles vaccination and characteristics associated with timely vaccination following MCV2 introduction. Methods A secondary analysis from a 2021 cross-sectional household survey of children aged 12–35 months in Oromia, Ethiopia was conducted. MCV vaccination status and age at vaccination were determined from the child's vaccination card. The cumulative card-confirmed vaccination coverage of MCV1 and MCV2 (among children 24–35 months) by age at vaccination was estimated. Among children who received MCV, vaccination timing was classified as early (MCV1: <9 months; MCV2: <15 months), timely (MCV1: 9 to <10 months; MCV2: 15 to <16 months), or delayed (MCV1: ≥10 months; MCV2: ≥16 months). Characteristics associated with timely MCV1 vaccination were analyzed using multivariate logistic regression, with urban/rural stratification. Results Overall, 651 children aged 12–35 months (MCV1) and a subset of 270 children aged 24–35 months (MCV2) were analyzed. Cumulative MCV1 coverage was 59.9% by age 9 months and 76.3% by age 12 months, and MCV2 was 33.0% by age 15 months and 44.8% by age 24 months. MCV coverage was generally higher in urban compared to rural areas. Among vaccinated children, the proportion receiving early, timely, and delayed doses was 30.1%, 44.5%, and 25.3% for MCV1, and 28.6%, 41.2%, and 30.3% for MCV2, respectively. Characteristics associated with timely MCV1 vaccination differed in urban and rural areas, but common themes included increased caregiver immunization awareness and service delivery aspects. Conclusions Although most children who received MCV1 were vaccinated by 12 months, many received delayed doses. MCV2 coverage was low, irrespective of vaccination timing. Findings highlight the importance of routine catch-up vaccination policies and guidance, and the need for tailored strategies in urban and rural settings to improve MCV coverage and timely vaccination.

abstract_zh: 背景 延迟 麻疹 与含 麻疹 的 疫苗(MCV1、MCV2)的首剂/次剂量会增加 麻疹 传播 的风险。MCV2 于 2019 年被添加到埃塞俄比亚的常规免疫计划中,在 15 个月大时接种。我们描述了 麻疹 疫苗接种 的年龄以及与 MCV2 引入后及时 疫苗接种 相关的特征。方法 对 2021 年埃塞俄比亚奥罗米亚州 12-35 个月龄儿童进行的横断面家庭调查进行了二次分析。MCV 疫苗接种 状态和 疫苗接种 年龄是根据孩子的 疫苗接种 卡确定的。估计了按 疫苗接种 年龄划分的 MCV1 和 MCV2(24-35 个月儿童)的累积卡确认 疫苗接种 覆盖率。在接受 MCV 的儿童中,疫苗接种 时间分为早期(MCV1:<9 个月;MCV2:<15 个月)、及时(MCV1:9 至 <10 个月;MCV2:15 至 <16 个月)或延迟(MCV1:≥10 个月;MCV2:≥16 个月)。使用多元逻辑回归和城市/农村分层分析与及时 MCV1 疫苗接种 相关的特征。结果 总体而言,对 651 名 12-35 个月的儿童 (MCV1) 和 270 名 24-35 个月的儿童 (MCV2) 进行了分析。9 个月时的累积 MCV1 覆盖率为 59.9%,12 个月时为 76.3%,15 个月时的 MCV2 累积覆盖率为 33.0%,24 个月时为 44.8%。与农村地区相比,城市地区的 MCV 覆盖率普遍较高。接种儿童中,MCV1 早期接种、及时接种和延迟接种比例分别为 30.1%、44.5% 和 25.3%,MCV2 接种比例分别为 28.6%、41.2% 和 30.3%。与及时 MCV1 疫苗接种 相关的特征在城市和农村地区有所不同,但共同主题包括护理人员免疫意识和服务提供方面的提高。结论 虽然大多数接受 MCV1 的儿童在 12 个月大时就接种了疫苗,但许多人接受了延迟剂量。无论 疫苗接种 时间如何,MCV2 覆盖率都很低。研究结果强调了常规追赶疫苗接种政策和指导的重要性,以及在城乡环境中制定量身定制的策略以提高MCV覆盖率和及时疫苗接种的必要性。

full_text: Abstract Introduction Infections caused by measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) can lead to severe illness and complications among people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). This study aimed to evaluate the seroprevalence of MMR and VZV among people living with HIV and provide data to support proactive immunization strategies. Materials and Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included adults living with HIV who were followed up at the infectious diseases and clinical microbiology outpatient clinic between October 2020 and December 2025. Demographic characteristics, baseline CD4+ T-cell counts, and MMR and VZV immunoglobulin G serology results were assessed. Vaccination indications were evaluated according to current guideline recommendations. Results A total of 206 patients were included in the study. Of these, 91.3% were male, and the median age was 34 years. Seronegativity rates were 16.8% for measles, 12.9% for mumps, 9.1% for rubella, and 3.4% for VZV. An indication for MMR vaccination was identified in 27.2% of patients, whereas 3.4% had an indication for VZV vaccination. Seronegativity increased with age for rubella but decreased with age for the other viruses. Conclusion A substantial immunity gap for MMR persists among people living with HIV, whereas VZV seropositivity remains high. Assessment of serological immunity and vaccination of eligible patients should be integral components of HIV care. Introduction With the introduction of antiretroviral therapy, the life expectancy and quality of life of people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have improved significantly[1, 2]. However, the immunosuppressive effects of HIV infection may increase susceptibility to vaccine-preventable infections and result in more severe clinical manifestations of these infections[3, 4]. Several studies have demonstrated that people living with HIV have lower seropositivity rates for measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), and varicella-zoster virus (VZV)[5, 6]. Accordingly, the European AIDS Clinical Society (EACS) guidelines recommend a proactive approach to screening and vaccination among people living with HIV[7]. In Türkiye, data on serological immunity to these vaccine-preventable infections among people living with HIV are limited. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the seroprevalence of MMR and VZV among people living with HIV, identify individuals eligible for vaccination, and contribute to the development of proactive immunization strategies. Materials and Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included all adults living with HIV who were followed up at the Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology outpatient clinic of University of Health Sciences Türkiye, Konya City Hospital between October 1, 2020, and December 31, 2025. Demographic data, including age, sex, education level, and route of HIV transmission, were recorded. Clinical and laboratory variables included baseline CD4+ T-cell count, baseline CD4 percentage, and serological markers for measles immunoglobulin G (IgG), mumps IgG, rubella IgG, and VZV IgG, which were obtained from patient records. Because measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines are administered as a combined MMR vaccine in Türkiye, MMR immunity was assessed collectively. Patients were considered to have an indication for MMR vaccination if seronegativity was detected for at least one available MMR serological marker (measles, mumps, or rubella IgG). Similarly, patients with a negative available VZV IgG result were considered to have an indication for varicella vaccination. Because serological testing was performed as part of routine clinical practice, complete serological data were not available for all patients. Therefore, vaccination indications were determined based on the available serological results, and unavailable serological results were not considered when determining vaccination indications. The serological markers were analyzed using enzyme-based immunoassay methods. HIV infection was defined as reactivity in an HIV type 1/2 (HIV-1/2) antigen/antibody assay and was subsequently confirmed using a rapid supplemental test performed at a central public health laboratory (Geenius HIV-1/2 Supplemental Assay, Bio-Rad Laboratories, Redmond, WA, USA). This study was approved by the University of Health Sciences Türkiye, Konya City Hospital Clinical Research Ethics Committee (approval number: 2026/89; April 13, 2026) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Given the retrospective cross-sectional design of the study, written informed consent was not obtained from the patients. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables were presented as means ± standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs; 25th-75th percentiles). As the continuous variables did not follow a normal distribution according to the Shapiro-Wilk test, nonparametric methods were used. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. For between-group comparisons, the Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally distributed continuous variables, and the chi-square test was used for categorical variables. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Chicago, IL, USA), and a p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results During the study period, 206 patients with HIV infection were identified from the outpatient clinic records. Of these patients, 188 (91.3%) were male, and the median age was 34 years (IQR, 27-44 years). The distribution of HIV transmission routes in the study population was as follows: heterosexual contact, 107 (51.9%); men who have sex with men (MSM), 29 (14.1%); intravenous drug use, 3 (1.5%); and unknown, 67 (32.5%). The median CD4+ T-cell count was 447 cells/mm3 (IQR, 301-627 cells/mm3), and the median CD4 percentage was 19.6% (IQR, 14.6%-27.0%) (Table 1). Measles serology was available for 190 patients (92.2%), mumps serology for 124 patients (60.2%), rubella serology for 198 patients (96.1%), and VZV serology for 179 patients (86.9%). Seropositivity rates were 83.2% for measles, 87.1% for mumps, 90.9% for rubella, and 96.6% for VZV (Table 1). Accordingly, seronegativity was observed in 16.8% of patients for measles, 12.9% for mumps, 9.1% for rubella, and 3.4% for VZV. Regarding the combined MMR vaccine, seronegativity to at least one available MMR component was detected in 27.2% of patients (56/206) based on the available serological results. These patients were considered to have an indication for MMR vaccination. The distribution of these patients is shown in Figure 1. Among patients with an indication for MMR vaccination, 89.3% (50 of 56) had a baseline CD4+ T-cell count ≥200 cells/μL, and all patients with an indication for VZV vaccination (6 patients) had a CD4+ T-cell count ≥200 cells/μL, indicating immunological eligibility for vaccination at the time of presentation. Among the 14 women of reproductive age (18-49 years), rubella IgG antibodies were negative in 4 (28.6%); 3 of these 4 patients had adequate baseline CD4+ T-cell counts (CD4+ ≥200 cells/μL) for vaccination. In addition, MMR and VZV serostatuses were analyzed according to the patients’ sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. Bivariate analysis showed no significant differences between groups in terms of sex, education level, MSM status, CD4+ T-cell count, or CD4 percentage. Rubella seronegativity increased with advancing age, whereas seronegativity for the other viruses decreased with age. These associations were statistically significant for all viruses except mumps (p < 0.05) (Table 2). The distribution of MMR and VZV IgG antibody positivity and negativity according to patients’ birth years is shown in Figure 2. Discussion In this study, the serostatus of MMR and varicella was evaluated in an adult cohort of people living with HIV in Türkiye. We found that 27.2% of patients were susceptible to at least one infection preventable by the MMR vaccine, and 3.4% were susceptible to VZV. The EACS guidelines and the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommend serological assessment of immunity to MMR and VZV in people living with HIV and vaccination of patients without evidence of immunity who have a CD4+ T-cell count ≥200 cells/mm3 or a CD4 percentage ≥15%[7, 8]. In our study, approximately 90% of patients with an indication for MMR vaccination and all patients with an indication for VZV vaccination had CD4+ T-cell counts appropriate for vaccination at the time of presentation, indicating that immunization strategies are generally clinically feasible. In Türkiye, measles vaccination was included in the national immunization program in 1970; a second dose was introduced for first-grade schoolchildren in 1998, and in 2006, the combined MMR vaccine was incorporated into routine immunization following the addition of mumps and rubella vaccines to the national immunization program[9]. Nevertheless, following migration movements associated with the civil war in Syria in 2011, increases in measles cases and periodic outbreaks have been reported in Türkiye, as in many European countries[3, 6, 9, 10]. This epidemiological change makes the assessment of measles susceptibility even more important, particularly in populations with limited immune protection. In our study, measles seronegativity among people living with HIV was 16.8%. This rate is considerably higher than those reported in HIV cohorts from European countries such as Germany (3.2%)[6], France (4.6%)[11], and the United Kingdom (7%)[3]. However, it is similar to the rate reported in a multicenter HIV cohort from Türkiye (18%)[12]. Considering that measles is associated with a more severe clinical course and increased mortality in individuals with T-cell immunodeficiency[13], this high susceptibility to measles among people living with HIV in our country represents an important public health risk. Our study also demonstrated a statistically significant association between age and measles serostatus. According to the birth cohort analysis, measles seronegativity was 0% among patients born between 1950 and 1960, whereas this rate progressively increased in subsequent birth cohorts, reaching 50% among those born between 2001 and 2010. This finding may be explained by stronger and more durable immunity among individuals in older birth cohorts, who were more likely to have acquired immunity through natural infection, whereas in younger cohorts, vaccine-induced immunity may wane over time or the primary vaccine response may be insufficient[14, 15]. Similarly, previous studies have reported higher measles seropositivity among older age groups and increased susceptibility among younger adults living with HIV[3, 6, 9-11]. Although there is no strong evidence that mumps or rubella infections have a more severe clinical course in people living with HIV, rubella infection during pregnancy may result in serious fetal and neonatal complications; therefore, maintaining rubella immunity remains clinically and epidemiologically important for women living with HIV[4]. In our study, 12.9% of adults living with HIV were seronegative for mumps, and 9.1% were seronegative for rubella. Furthermore, 28.6% of women of reproductive age were seronegative for rubella, which is noteworthy. This rate is higher than those reported in cohorts of HIV-positive women of reproductive age from Iran (17.3%)[4], Austria (18.2%)[16], and Germany (9%)[6]. However, because the number of female patients in our study was limited, these comparisons should be interpreted with caution. In our cohort, unlike the other three viruses, rubella seronegativity increased with advancing age. A similar trend was observed in another HIV cohort from Türkiye, although the association did not reach statistical significance[12]. In contrast, a cohort from Germany showed decreasing seronegativity with increasing age[6]. These differences may be attributable to historical variations in vaccination schedules, vaccination coverage rates, and the circulation of natural infection between countries. It is well known that VZV infections, related complications, and mortality occur more frequently among people living with HIV[17, 18]. In our study, VZV seropositivity was detected in 96.6% of patients. Since the varicella vaccine was incorporated into the national immunization program in Türkiye in 2013[19], the high seropositivity observed in our adult cohort is likely attributable primarily to a history of natural infection rather than vaccination. Nevertheless, although seropositivity indicates protection against varicella infection, VZV reactivation and its associated clinical manifestations cannot be completely excluded in people living with HIV because of impaired cellular immunity[20, 21]. Study Limitations This study has some limitations. First, the single-center, retrospective design may limit the generalizability of the findings. Furthermore, because serological tests were performed as part of routine clinical practice, complete MMR serological data were not available for all patients. Therefore, indications for MMR vaccination were determined based on the available serological results, and the reported prevalence may have underestimated the true prevalence. In addition, reliable data on the vaccination history of most patients were unavailable. Therefore, seronegativity cannot be attributed solely to a lack of vaccination; it may also reflect waning vaccine-induced immunity, primary vaccine failure, or HIV-related immune dysfunction. However, this study was not designed to determine the underlying causes of seronegativity but rather to evaluate serological immunity to MMR and VZV among people living with HIV. Despite these limitations, this study has important strengths. First, it is one of the few studies evaluating both MMR and VZV immunity among people living with HIV in Türkiye. Second, it includes a large adult cohort spanning multiple birth cohorts, providing valuable epidemiological insights into the national context. Conclusion In conclusion, our study demonstrates an immunity gap for MMR components among adults living with HIV, whereas VZV seropositivity remains high. These findings support the need for systematic assessment of immunity to vaccine-preventable infections as part of HIV care and vaccination of eligible patients in accordance with current guidelines.

full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Introduction Infections caused by measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) can lead to severe illness and complications among people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). This study aimed to evaluate the seroprevalence of MMR and VZV among people living with HIV and provide data to support proactive immunization strategies. Materials and Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included adults living with HIV who were followed up at the infectious diseases and clinical microbiology outpatient clinic between October 2020 and December 2025. Demographic characteristics, baseline CD4+ T-cell counts, and MMR and VZV immunoglobulin G serology results were assessed. Vaccination indications were evaluated according to current guideline recommendations. Results A total of 206 patients were included in the study. Of these, 91.3% were male, and the median age was 34 years. Seronegativity rates were 16.8% for measles, 12.9% for mumps, 9.1% for rubella, and 3.4% for VZV. An indication for MMR vaccination was identified in 27.2% of patients, whereas 3.4% had an indication for VZV vaccination. Seronegativity increased with age for rubella but decreased with age for the other viruses. Conclusion A substantial immunity gap for MMR persists among people living with HIV, whereas VZV seropositivity remains high. Assessment of serological immunity and vaccination of eligible patients should be integral components of HIV care. Introduction With the introduction of antiretroviral therapy, the life expectancy and quality of life of people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have improved significantly[1, 2]. However, the immunosuppressive effects of HIV infection may increase susceptibility to vaccine-preventable infections and result in more severe clinical manifestations of these infections[3, 4]. Several studies have demonstrated that people living with HIV have lower seropositivity rates for measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), and varicella-zoster virus (VZV)[5, 6]. Accordingly, the European AIDS Clinical Society (EACS) guidelines recommend a proactive approach to screening and vaccination among people living with HIV[7]. In Türkiye, data on serological immunity to these vaccine-preventable infections among people living with HIV are limited. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the seroprevalence of MMR and VZV among people living with HIV, identify individuals eligible for vaccination, and contribute to the development of proactive immunization strategies. Materials and Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included all adults living with HIV who were followed up at the Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology outpatient clinic of University of Health Sciences Türkiye, Konya City Hospital between October 1, 2020, and December 31, 2025. Demographic data, including age, sex, education level, and route of HIV transmission, were recorded. Clinical and laboratory variables included baseline CD4+ T-cell count, baseline CD4 percentage, and serological markers for measles immunoglobulin G (IgG), mumps IgG, rubella IgG, and VZV IgG, which were obtained from patient records. Because measles, mumps, and rubella vaccines are administered as a combined MMR vaccine in Türkiye, MMR immunity was assessed collectively. Patients were considered to have an indication for MMR vaccination if seronegativity was detected for at least one available MMR serological marker (measles, mumps, or rubella IgG). Similarly, patients with a negative available VZV IgG result were considered to have an indication for varicella vaccination. Because serological testing was performed as part of routine clinical practice, complete serological data were not available for all patients. Therefore, vaccination indications were determined based on the available serological results, and unavailable serological results were not considered when determining vaccination indications. The serological markers were analyzed using enzyme-based immunoassay methods. HIV infection was defined as reactivity in an HIV type 1/2 (HIV-1/2) antigen/antibody assay and was subsequently confirmed using a rapid supplemental test performed at a central public health laboratory (Geenius HIV-1/2 Supplemental Assay, Bio-Rad Laboratories, Redmond, WA, USA). This study was approved by the University of Health Sciences Türkiye, Konya City Hospital Clinical Research Ethics Committee (approval number: 2026/89; April 13, 2026) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Given the retrospective cross-sectional design of the study, written informed consent was not obtained from the patients. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables were presented as means ± standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs; 25th-75th percentiles). As the continuous variables did not follow a normal distribution according to the Shapiro-Wilk test, nonparametric methods were used. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. For between-group comparisons, the Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally distributed continuous variables, and the chi-square test was used for categorical variables. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Chicago, IL, USA), and a p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results During the study period, 206 patients with HIV infection were identified from the outpatient clinic records. Of these patients, 188 (91.3%) were male, and the median age was 34 years (IQR, 27-44 years). The distribution of HIV transmission routes in the study population was as follows: heterosexual contact, 107 (51.9%); men who have sex with men (MSM), 29 (14.1%); intravenous drug use, 3 (1.5%); and unknown, 67 (32.5%). The median CD4+ T-cell count was 447 cells/mm3 (IQR, 301-627 cells/mm3), and the median CD4 percentage was 19.6% (IQR, 14.6%-27.0%) (Table 1). Measles serology was available for 190 patients (92.2%), mumps serology for 124 patients (60.2%), rubella serology for 198 patients (96.1%), and VZV serology for 179 patients (86.9%). Seropositivity rates were 83.2% for measles, 87.1% for mumps, 90.9% for rubella, and 96.6% for VZV (Table 1). Accordingly, seronegativity was observed in 16.8% of patients for measles, 12.9% for mumps, 9.1% for rubella, and 3.4% for VZV. Regarding the combined MMR vaccine, seronegativity to at least one available MMR component was detected in 27.2% of patients (56/206) based on the available serological results. These patients were considered to have an indication for MMR vaccination. The distribution of these patients is shown in Figure 1. Among patients with an indication for MMR vaccination, 89.3% (50 of 56) had a baseline CD4+ T-cell count ≥200 cells/μL, and all patients with an indication for VZV vaccination (6 patients) had a CD4+ T-cell count ≥200 cells/μL, indicating immunological eligibility for vaccination at the time of presentation. Among the 14 women of reproductive age (18-49 years), rubella IgG antibodies were negative in 4 (28.6%); 3 of these 4 patients had adequate baseline CD4+ T-cell counts (CD4+ ≥200 cells/μL) for vaccination. In addition, MMR and VZV serostatuses were analyzed according to the patients’ sociodemographic and clinical characteristics.
